arc.canonicalText: She brought her young son to live with her after his foster mother became ill. She was twenty-two. He had spent his first three years with that other family. They were the home he knew.
arc.sourceNote: Chronology summary, not a staged arrival. Estate date is January1930; the exact place and day of the remembered chair episode are not supplied.

arc.canonicalText: Years later, she remembered him lying across a chair and crying quietly. He was losing the family he had known.
arc.sourceNote: Primary memoir excerpt explicitly memory-framed. No continuous-room claim, invented touch or inferred guilt.

arc.canonicalText: He stayed with her in the room she rented. Mother and child lived together for several months.
arc.sourceNote: STRUCTURAL EXCEPTION: documented living arrangement, not an invented smallest response to the chair incident. Owning-estate chronology is secondary context, not a letter read.

arc.canonicalText: Her son was ill with a cough that kept him awake at night. She was also trying to manage her secretarial job. She could not keep the arrangement going.
arc.sourceNote: Estate narrative of practical care difficulty. No treatment guidance, invented failed comfort or diagnosis beyond the source's account.

arc.canonicalText: Her mother suggested that the child come to live at the family farm. She took him there.
arc.sourceNote: Secondary chronological account, not reconstructed dialogue or a newly documented decision scene. No first-person letter is claimed.

arc.canonicalText: His grandparents cared for him for more than a year. Much later, his mother wrote that the memory of his tears still hurt. She had not forgotten them.
arc.sourceNote: A bounded care consequence plus explicitly later recollection, not a claim that shared care erased distress or produced her fiction.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Astrid Lindgren.

She wrote children's books, including the stories about Pippi Longstocking.

Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You are allowed to have complicated feelings about needing help.
arc.sourceNote: Own-line reveal. No promise of reunion, advice or claim that a child's pain caused artistic greatness.
